As I tried to recall my schedule for the day, the word 'shutdowns' tumbled out of my mouth and echoed back at me from my mental dictionary, refusing to sit quietly. She had always loved coming back to college for summer breaks - the way the buildings sparkled like new after a fresh coat of paint; the smell of fresh-cut grass wafting from the courtyard. But today, even these small pleasures felt hollow.

Emma wandered into the Student Union itself, searching for answers but also avoiding them. She wasn't sure if she was ready to face whatever truth lay ahead. After a few moments of awkward browsing, she spotted an acquaintance working behind the counter and joined the line, asking out of earshot about the possibility of the school closing down.

"Closed? Like what are you talking about?" His voice sounded confused, but the hesitation that followed made her think he knew exactly what she was referring to.

When it was my turn to pay, my mind wandered. What would happen if our college really did shut down? Her hand trembled ever so slightly as I handed over cash for a coffee I didn't even want.

He flopped onto his back and ran a hand through his hair, not even bothering to try to style it anymore. Every attempt felt futile without a destination - no graduation date on the horizon, no new place to hang out with friends as long-term roommates, no school lunches or late-night pizza runs.

Eventually he got dressed in sweats, avoiding looking outside at the rain-soaked streets, then headed downstairs for something hot to drink. His dad was making dinner and didn't mention anything specific - maybe because he thought Alex didn't want confirmation yet?

Alex poured milk into his cereal quietly; usually he added a big dollop but not today, like even this simple pleasure didn't deserve celebration anymore.

This time though... something's amiss. Not just because we know a lot of classes might be affected - if we even get to take them. Her heart seemed like it had dropped; its usual steady hum felt more labored as she turned back into her apartment to face some kind of official-looking letter on the kitchen counter, a notice about something happening this Friday.

With heavy steps I walked back over to the Student Union so we could see if there were any announcements up. They always used the board on Fridays; might as well check out of curiosity and solidarity with our school's staff who truly believe they can turn things around.

But it's hard for a 'feasible' plan now that things are getting more and more out of control at college - I can see our new president, well-intentioned as he is, getting bogged down by money, enrollment figures... whatever exactly this latest crisis relates to.

No sound came from his cup; he only managed crumbs off a stale biscuit after too many sips. The coffee machine here is probably more reliable than either school officials or our local economy at this rate...

For two years you lived here with your art projects, teaching students at the very spot outside where college had taken away all this sense of belonging. She sat in silence for so long that when someone from maintenance finally came by, Lena asked them straight out what kind of future lay ahead now: "Do we still finish up courses?" The look on his face said it wasn't even worth finishing, and she couldn't blame him.

As he walked out with some dusty vacuum cleaner, I sat alone among things I'd started - sketches of possible paintings that felt a long time coming – probably will never happen at all now.

Her fingers drummed a furious rhythm on her thighs, and she almost didn't notice her feet carrying her away from the scene.

Her classmates were already gathering near the parking lot, discussing their next move. Sarah stood apart, nursing a scalding tea from the cafeteria in desperate need of something tangible to hang onto. She glared at a cluster of junior year majors huddled around a phone, scrolling through their social media updates with what looked suspiciously like smugness. Her heart was racing, each beat throbbing like a challenge.

"Why didn't anyone tell me?" she shouted toward them, almost but not quite regretting the outburst right away. The group fell silent, and for an instant, they stared at her with something resembling pity instead of the usual camaraderie. Sarah's eyes flashed to the empty seats surrounding her – hers would soon be a vacant chair in a ghost college.

Kyle's feet pounded the pavement with an intensity that made heads turn, though he barely registered them. On the far side of the administration building, crowds were forming around bulletin boards and scattered handouts – details on campus closures and next steps.

For some reason, seeing so many students clustered in one spot, murmuring amongst themselves, just plain got to him. He took an impromptu detour into the empty courtyard behind Student Union, where the stark walls amplified every echo of his footsteps as he circled back onto himself. Why were decisions made without anyone to break them? Wasn't that what college was – a chance for them all to be there together?

Kyle paused beside a weathered fountain that'd stopped working months ago. No sound spilled out from it, its waterless basin staring up at him like an open mouth. That's when the rage bubbled over, or in his chest if not words. His fists clenched by his side before releasing with what could have been a sob. A bystander passed, giving him a fleeting glance – something that didn't quite amount to curiosity.

Upon reaching her own front door, Emma couldn't recall putting the spare keys outside – it was then that a cold numbness hit like an unannounced storm cloud rolling over her shoulders.

For what felt like several uneasy breaths afterward, she'd do nothing but fiddle with the lock while half-expecting some stranger's laugh to echo through the hallway. There was no answer. The sudden stillness only irritated Emma further; why was it always silence when people started discussing their problems?

Marcus bit back another furious outburst and instead forced his eyes upward from the spreading stain on the carpet – there weren't supposed to be decisions made like these by people behind a desk who'd never shown such reckless disdain for everyone sitting before them but he couldn't make more noise right now even if...

They seemed to seep back through her now – maybe this wasn't the end just yet, or rather, it would never be truly over because some moments left an invisible piece of their impact behind...
